title: Latency regret and priority threshold heuristic notebook
body:
Purpose / quick summary:
This doc collects experiments and notes testing a small, operational heuristic that uses a "latency-regret" signal to gate priority thresholds for continuous batch coalescing. Goal: reduce p99/p999 tail latency without sacrificing throughput/cost targets for mixed-priority workloads.

Why "regret"?
- Observed problem: using fixed timeouts+batch caps either gives good throughput (with large batches) or low median latency, but p99 explodes under microbursts and priority mixes.
- We define latency_regret per request class as: regret = max(0, observed_latency - baseline_target_ms). baseline_target_ms is SLAs per priority (eg 50ms for interactive, 200ms for background). Regret accumulation indicates when to tighten batching.

Hypothesis:
- If we dynamically reduce max_batch_size and flush timeouts for an affinity slot when regret accumulates above a threshold, we can reduce high-quantile latency while keeping overall token efficiency similar by only constraining problematic slots.

Experiment environment:
- Model: open-7b-llama-style quantized variant (int8 routes) on 2xA100 logical cluster (dedicated pool).
- Serving runtime: commit sha: 5f3b2c0 (profiling hooks, per-slot regret counters).
- Synthetic traces: poisson_base (lambda=30 req/s), chat-burst (bursts 500rps for 300ms every 20s), long-tail-lengths (60% short 8-64 tokens, 40% long 512-1024 tokens).
- Priority classes: interactive (p1), standard (p2), background (p3). Proportion: 25/60/15.
- Baseline config: static timeout 20ms, max_batch 128, fairness demotion: 2 levels.

Heuristic (prototype):
- For each slot, maintain regret_window = sum(regret) over 60s decaying with tau=30s.
- If regret_window > R_high -> set max_batch = max(8, floor(max_batch_current * 0.5)) and timeout_ms = max(2, timeout_ms * 0.5). Mark slot in "tight" mode for 30s.
- If regret_window < R_low for 60s -> slowly relax to default (increase batch by +10% every 30s until default).
- Priority thresholding: only enable tight mode automatically for slots where >40% of recent requests are priority p1. For p3-heavy slots, prefer increased batching to preserve throughput.

Runs and high-level results (summary):
- Run A (baseline static): p50=32ms, p95=180ms, p99=420ms, p999=1210ms, throughput=steady 850 tokens/s
- Run B (aggressive fixed small batches for all): p50=45ms, p95=95ms, p99=140ms, p999=320ms, throughput down 22% and cost/token up 18%
- Run C (regret heuristic, R_high=5000ms, R_low=1000ms): p50=34ms, p95=120ms, p99=165ms, p999=290ms, throughput -6%, cost/token +3%
- Run D (regret heuristic + priority gating): p50=33ms, p95=110ms, p99=150ms, p999=260ms, throughput -4%, cost/token +2%

Observations / profiling notes:
- The regret heuristic triggered mostly during the chat-burst windows and for slots where interactive requests concentrated. This reduced serialization delay for those requests and lowered tail latency substantially versus baseline without fully reducing batch size cluster-wide.
- Kernel-level profiling (nvprof snapshots) shows fewer long queue-waits on the host side for tight-mode batches; however GPU utilization had small dips (~3–6%) during tight-mode transitions.
- Cache hits (KV cache) are slightly worse for tight-mode because more flushes prevent cache reuse across batched requests; measured KV cache miss rate increased by ~4 percentage points for affected slots.

Failure modes / surprising behaviors:
- Oscillation: naive R_high/R_low choice produced on/off oscillations in a subset of slots (tight->relax->tight every ~70s). Fixed by introducing hysteresis (minimum tight duration 30s) and exponential backoff on relax steps.
- Priority misclassification: when p1 fraction estimate lags (sampling window too long), tight-mode was delayed. Shortening the priority sample window from 60s->10s improved responsiveness but increased noise — we balanced with a 10s median filter.
- Long-request coupling: in mixed-length slots, reducing batch size to protect p1 requests increased serialized overhead for long requests, causing them to be slower overall. Mitigation: apply token-length-weighted regret (weight long requests higher in regret accumulation so we only tighten if both latency-sensitive and long requests suffer).

Microbench numbers (selected traces, Run C):
- During burst period (20s window): average slot queue depth fell from 42->12 in tight-mode; observed median queue-wait 11ms->3ms.
- p99 measured on interactive requests during burst: 780ms->160ms.

Operational considerations:
- Telemetry: add a "regret_index" time series per slot, expose triggers and tight-mode toggles in Console with annotation links to trace ids.
- Rollout plan: start as an opt-in runtime flag in canary pool; enable for 10% traffic for 2 weeks; evaluate cost metrics and user-facing error/latency regressions.
- Safety: automatic fallback to default config if tight-mode reduces throughput below 60% of baseline for a sustained 5m window.

Open questions / next experiments:
- Can we compute regret without strongly relying on SLA baselines? (learned baseline from recent quantiles?)
- Evaluate longer decay windows for regret to handle diurnal shifts.
- Try combining with admission control: when regret large, shed background requests to preserve p1 SLOs instead of only tightening batch config.
- Test on more model families (causal vs encoder-decoder) — batching impact differs for long-output workloads.

Action items:
- [ ] Add regression test that runs synthetic burst traces and asserts p99 reduction for p1 class > 50% vs baseline (Ravi)
- [ ] Instrument console panels for regret_index and tight-mode annotations (Lina)
- [ ] Create canary rollout PR and safety kill-switch (Maya)

Appendix: useful commands / traces used (notes)
- kickoff: ./tools/sim-trace --trace chat-burst.json --mix 25:60:15 --commit 5f3b2c0
- collect: python tools/collect_metrics.py --commit 5f3b2c0 --metrics p50,p95,p99,p999,kv-miss,throughput --out runC.csv
- nvprof snapshot: nvprof --profile-child-processes --csv -o nv_runC.csv ./serve --slot-id 12 --tight-mode

Notes to self: keep tuning R_high in powers of two; start conservative. This heuristic looks promising operationally because it localizes decisions to slots and is cheap to compute in the runtime.
